hieu-nguyen-duc.name: Nguyen Duc Hieu
paragraphs: Three Trousers. One Very Long Day.
There was a time when Nguyen Duc Hieu could spend as many as 18 hours at his workbench.
At the end of that day, he might have completed only three pairs of trousers.
Not thirty.
Three.
That number tells you something important about the kind of tailoring Hieu has practiced throughout his career.
This is not mass production.
It is a craft where precision takes time.
From Making Trousers to Teaching Others
Long before joining Dunnio, Hieu had already spent years mastering the construction of tailored trousers.
His technical knowledge eventually led him to another role: teaching the craft to other tailors in large tailoring workshops in Hanoi.
Teaching changes the way a craftsman understands his profession.
It is no longer enough to know how to do something.
You have to understand why it works.
Why does a trouser leg fall cleanly?
Why does one waistband sit comfortably while another twists?
Why does the fabric pull in one direction?
Why can two pairs of trousers made from the same measurements feel completely different when worn?
For Hieu, these questions have been answered through years at the workbench — making, observing, correcting and teaching.
A Good Pair of Trousers Should Look Effortless
Trousers are often the quietest part of a suit.
There are no lapels to attract attention. No dramatic shoulders. No complex front construction for the customer to admire.
And that is precisely why they are difficult to make well.
When tailored correctly, a pair of trousers should simply fall beautifully.
The waistband should sit naturally.
The seat should follow the body without unnecessary tension.
The crease should remain clean.
The legs should create a sharp, balanced line from waist to shoe.
When everything is right, most people will never notice the work behind it.
They will simply notice that the trousers look right.
That simplicity requires precision.
The Millimeters That Matter
Experienced trouser makers learn to see details that most people overlook.
A small adjustment at the waist.
A little more room through the seat.
The relationship between the hips, thighs and knees.
The way a particular fabric responds when the wearer walks or sits.
A few millimeters can change the entire balance of a pair of trousers.
This is where decades of experience matter.
Hieu does not simply sew pieces of fabric together.
He reads the structure of the garment as it takes shape.
He watches the lines.
He feels the tension.
He corrects what does not sit naturally.
And he continues until the trousers have the clean, precise appearance he expects from his own work.
Still at the Workbench
Perhaps the most remarkable thing about Hieu's story is not that he once taught other tailors.
It is that he still makes trousers himself.
Day after day.
Pair after pair.
The tools have improved.
Technology has changed the way orders reach the workshop.
Dunnio can now receive information from customers far beyond Vietnam.
But when the fabric reaches Hieu's workbench, the fundamental process remains remarkably human.
A craftsman.
A sewing machine.
A piece of fabric.
And years of knowledge guiding every decision.
Some Things Should Not Be Rushed
At Dunnio, technology helps us move information faster.
But craftsmanship follows a different clock.
There are moments when speed matters.
And there are moments when taking more time creates something better.
Hieu's work reminds us of that distinction.
A handcrafted pair of trousers may require hundreds of individual decisions before it is finished.
That is why, even after decades in the profession, he continues to approach his work with the same discipline:
Measure carefully. Sew precisely. Look again. Correct if necessary.
And then move on to the next pair.
The Hands Behind Dunnio
When you order a tailored garment from Dunnio, technology may help communicate your measurements, preferences and design choices across thousands of miles.
But technology does not sit at this workbench.
Hieu does.
Behind the digital experience is a real craftsman in Vietnam who has spent decades understanding how trousers should fit, move and fall.
That is the relationship we want to preserve at Dunnio:
Technology connects us. Craftsmanship completes the garment.
Nguyen Duc Hieu Master Trouser Maker — Dunnio
One Craftsman. One Pair at a Time. Made in Vietnam.

doan-tran-van.name: Tran Van Doan
paragraphs: A Craft Learned by Hand
For Tran Van Doan, tailoring was never simply a profession he chose later in life.
He began learning to sew when he was still a child.

As a young apprentice, he followed the traditional path into the trade — observing experienced tailors, assisting with their work, practicing repeatedly, and gradually learning to understand a garment not only through measurements, but through his hands.
He later trained and worked as an apprentice at Phu Hung Tailor in Hanoi , where he continued developing his skills in traditional tailoring.
It was the kind of education that cannot be rushed.
Watch. Practice. Make mistakes. Correct them. And do it again.
Over more than three decades, those repetitions became experience.
And experience became craftsmanship.
The Jacket Is Where Experience Matters
Today, Doan specializes in the handcrafted construction of suit jackets — one of the most demanding parts of traditional tailoring.
A jacket may look simple when it is finished.
Behind that simplicity are countless decisions.
How should the fabric behave around the shoulder?
How should the chest be shaped?
How should the lapel roll?
How should the jacket balance when the wearer stands, walks or moves?
Different fabrics respond differently. Different bodies require different adjustments. And more complicated designs demand an understanding that goes far beyond following a standard pattern.
After more than 30 years at the workbench, Doan has worked with a wide range of fabrics, constructions and tailoring styles, including highly complex suit designs.
His experience allows him to adapt his technique to the garment in front of him rather than expecting every garment to behave the same way.
Some Knowledge Lives in the Hands
Modern technology can help us measure more accurately, manage orders more efficiently and connect Dunnio with customers thousands of miles away.
But there is another kind of knowledge that is much harder to digitize.
It is knowing how much tension a particular fabric needs.
Knowing when a seam does not sit quite right.
Feeling how a jacket should be shaped before the customer ever puts it on.
Recognizing a small problem before it becomes visible in the finished garment.
These instincts are not learned from a manual.
They are built through decades of making clothes.
That is the knowledge Doan brings to every jacket he works on.
More Than 30 Years. One Garment at a Time.
At Dunnio, we believe technology and craftsmanship should not compete with each other.
Technology should make tailoring more accessible.
Craftsmanship should make it worth wearing.
When a Dunnio customer places an order digitally, the journey may begin with technology — but eventually the fabric reaches the hands of people.
People who cut.
People who shape.
People who sew.
People who have spent much of their lives understanding how a garment should be made.
Tran Van Doan is one of those people.
For more than three decades, he has practiced the same craft.
Today, as a Master Tailor specializing in handcrafted suit jackets, his experience becomes part of every garment that passes through his hands.
Because behind a well-made jacket, there should always be someone who understands how to make it.
Tran Van Doan Master Tailor — Handcrafted Suit Jackets
30+ Years of Craftsmanship. Made in Vietnam.

duy-dat-nguyen.name: Nguyen Duy Dat
paragraphs: From a Small Tailoring Shop in Hanoi to a Global Vision
Nguyen Duy Dat Founder & CEO, Dunnio
In 2009, I opened a small tailoring shop in Hanoi with a simple belief: if we wanted customers to trust us, we had to make clothes we were genuinely proud of.
We did not have a large factory, a famous name, or sophisticated technology. What we had was craftsmanship, persistence, and a willingness to remake a garment when it was not good enough.
That principle has stayed with me ever since.
Make it well. Keep improving. Never take the customer's trust for granted.
Learning the Craft
My journey in tailoring began with studying fashion design at the Hanoi College of Textile and Garment and continued through years of hands-on experience.
I learned that a well-made suit is not simply about measurements.
It is about understanding the person who will wear it — their body, preferences, profession, occasion, and how they want to feel when they put it on.
Over the years, our small shop grew into a tailoring business serving thousands of customers.
But growth also taught me something important:
Craftsmanship alone is not enough to build the future of tailoring.
Why Tailoring Needs Technology
Traditional tailoring is deeply personal, but it is also difficult to scale.
A customer normally has to visit a tailor, choose a fabric, explain what they want, have their measurements taken, return for fittings, and wait for the garment to be completed.
I began asking a different question:
What if we could preserve the craftsmanship of traditional tailoring while making the entire experience simpler through technology?
That question eventually became one of the foundations of Dunnio.
Today, we are building a tailoring system that connects craftsmanship, production, customer data, digital customization, measurement technology, e-commerce and our own ERP infrastructure.
The goal is simple:
Make personalized tailoring easier to access — wherever you live.
Made in Vietnam. Designed for the World.
Vietnam has a long tradition of skilled garment making.
I believe that capability deserves greater recognition internationally.
Dunnio is therefore not simply about selling suits overseas.
We want to build a system that allows customers around the world to access the craftsmanship of Vietnamese tailors through a modern, convenient and transparent experience.

Customers should be able to explore fabrics, personalize their garments, provide measurements and place orders digitally — while the actual garment is carefully produced and quality-controlled by experienced people in Vietnam.
Technology makes the process possible.
People make the product meaningful.
Real Craftsmanship. Real People.
As technology and artificial intelligence become more powerful, I believe authenticity will become even more valuable.
That is why Dunnio will continue to show the real people behind our products.
The people who cut the fabric.
The people who sew the garments.
The people who inspect the fit and finishing.
The people who solve problems when something does not go as planned.
We do not believe that tailoring should become a completely automated, anonymous transaction.
Technology should remove friction.
It should not remove the human craftsmanship behind the garment.
Building for the Long Term
I have spent more than 17 years in this industry, and one lesson has become increasingly clear:
A company can grow quickly because of an opportunity. A brand lasts because people trust it.

That trust has to be earned through thousands of small decisions — how we make a garment, how honestly we communicate, how we handle mistakes, and whether we are willing to improve when something is not good enough.
That is the company I want Dunnio to become.
Not the cheapest tailor.
Not simply another fashion brand.
But a trusted tailoring company from Vietnam that combines craftsmanship, technology and responsible production to serve customers around the world.
Our Journey Is Just Beginning
What started as a small tailoring shop in Hanoi in 2009 has become a much bigger ambition.
We are building toward a future where a customer in New York, London, Sydney, Tokyo or anywhere else can order a personalized garment from Vietnam with confidence.
And behind that garment will still be something deeply human:
the hands, skills and pride of the people who made it.
That is the future of tailoring I believe in.
And that is the future we are building at Dunnio.
Nguyen Duy Dat Founder & CEO DUNNIO
Made in Vietnam. Made for You.
